Second Helvetic Confession
SEK-uhnd hel-VET-ik kuhn-FESH-uhn
noun (confessional standard)
From Latin Helvetia (Switzerland) + confession; the second of the great Swiss Reformed confessions, written by Heinrich Bullinger in 1561 and published in 1566.

Biblical Definition

The Second Helvetic Confession is the mature confession of the Swiss Reformed churches, composed privately by Heinrich Bullinger — Zwingli's successor at Zurich — in 1561 as his own testimony of faith, and published in 1566 when Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate, under attack for his Reformed convictions, sought a clear statement to defend himself before the imperial diet. It was at once received across the Reformed world: Switzerland, the Palatinate, Scotland, Hungary, Poland, France. Of all the Reformation confessions it had the widest reception. Its thirty chapters open with Scripture as the true Word of God and the rule of faith, declare the preaching of that Word to be the Word of God, and move through the Trinity, providence, predestination, the fall, free will's bondage, justification by faith, the church, the sacraments, and the Christian magistrate. Its tone is warm and pastoral as well as precise, framing doctrine for the comfort and order of the church. This dictionary honors it as one of the chief Reformed standards, kin to the Heidelberg Catechism with which it was so often bound, and as a faithful witness to the sovereign grace the 1689 Confession also professes.

Webster 1828 Definition

The mature Swiss Reformed confession, written by Heinrich Bullinger in 1561 and published in 1566; the most widely received of the Reformation confessions, opening with Scripture and the preaching of the Word, and confessing the Trinity, predestination, and justification by faith.

SECOND HELVETIC CONFESSION, noun. The confession of the Swiss Reformed churches, written by Heinrich Bullinger (1561), published 1566.

The most widely received Reformation confession — adopted in Switzerland, the Palatinate, Scotland, Hungary, Poland, and beyond.

Thirty chapters opening with Holy Scripture as the Word of God and rule of faith.

Declares the preached Word of God to be the Word of God to the hearer.

Confesses the Trinity, predestination, justification by faith, and the Christian magistrate.

Key Scripture

Rom 10:17 — "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God."

2 Pet 1:21 — "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love."

John 17:17 — "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth."

Modern Corruption

This confession faces little redefinition, being a settled historic text; the live danger is forgetting it altogether — a Reformed world that prizes novelty and neglects the rich witness of its own confessions, leaving its people unanchored against the doctrines of the age.

expand to see more

Where the Second Helvetic Confession is corrupted today is chiefly by neglect. Many who name themselves Reformed have never read it, and a church ignorant of its confessions is easy prey for every wind of doctrine (Eph 4:14). Bullinger's clear word that the preached Scripture is the very Word of God rebukes a generation that has traded preaching for performance and the Bible for the felt needs of the hour.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; its text is fixed and public. The principle to recover is the confession's own opening conviction: that Holy Scripture is the true Word of God, sufficient and authoritative, and that faith comes by the hearing of that Word (Rom 10:17). The widest-received confession of the Reformation calls the church back to the Book it was written to defend.
